turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Doctor. It's nice to meet you. Well, my daughter actually drove me here today, which was lovely of her, though we hit simply dreadful traffic on the way over. They've been doing construction on that main road since... oh, it must be 1998? I remember because my late husband bought his blue Buick that year, such a boat of a car, and he hated getting dust on it. 

But anyway, you asked why I'm here. Well, for the past year or so, I just feel like I’m always puttering around the house. Fixing things, arranging the pantry, volunteering for just one more committee at the church. Speaking of the church, the spring bazaar was last weekend and I ended up making three dozen of my lemon bars because Margaret's arthritis is acting up, poor dear. She usually does the baking. 

But... yes, what brings me in is that even at 87, I just have a terribly hard time just sitting down and being still. I don't know why I can't just rest in my armchair like everyone else my age.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes constantly puttering, fixing, arranging, and volunteering, and explicitly states she has a terribly hard time sitting down and being still.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting in your armchair, do you feel sad or down in your mood, or do you find that things you normally enjoy—like your hobbies or time with family—just don't bring you pleasure anymore?
turns.patient_response:
Sad? Oh heavens, no. I wouldn't say I feel sad at all. I still love all my little projects and seeing my family. In fact, I was just trying to work on a cross-stitch for my youngest great-grandson while sitting in that armchair. 

It's a wonderful chair, by the way—a lovely floral wingback I found at an estate sale over on Maple Drive. The Henderson estate, I believe it was. They had the most magnificent collection of antique thimbles, just hundreds of them in these little wooden display cases, but I just bought the chair and a little silver tray. I actually polished that tray just yesterday... or was it Tuesday? Must have been Tuesday, because the mailman was running late and I was watching for him out the front window. He usually comes right at eleven, you know. 

But no, I don't feel down or blue in the slightest. I just can't seem to stay sitting in that lovely chair for more than a few minutes without popping back up to dust the tray or check the mail or what have you. So, no, I still enjoy my life quite a bit!

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an inability to stay seated for more than a few minutes without popping back up to do other things, indicating restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling sad, down, or blue.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly denies losing interest, stating she still loves her projects, seeing her family, and enjoys life quite a bit.

turns.doctor_question: When you feel that urge to get up and move around, do you notice your heart racing, or do your hands shake, or do you feel sweaty or uncomfortable in your body?
turns.patient_response:
My heart? Oh goodness, no, nothing like that. My heart is strong as a horse. I actually just saw my regular doctor, Dr. Evans, back in January—or maybe it was February? No, it was definitely January, right after that terrible ice storm that knocked out the power over on Elm Street. We had to use candles for two whole days, and I ended up burning through all my good beeswax tapers. They smelled just like fresh honey, which was lovely, but they drip so terribly if there's even the slightest draft in the hallway. 

But no, I don't get sweaty or shaky at all. My hands are still quite steady, thank heavens. You really must have steady hands for cross-stitching, you know. My mother taught me how to stitch when I was just a little girl. She had the most beautiful sewing box... solid cherry wood with these tiny little brass hinges. I think my sister Eleanor took it when she moved down to Florida in the seventies. Florida is just much too humid for me, speaking of sweating! 

So, no, I don't feel uncomfortable or panicky in my body or anything like that. I just... I just feel like I need to be up and doing something.

turns.doctor_question: When you feel that urge to get up and move around, do you also notice that you're worried or anxious about something, or does it feel more like a physical restlessness without any particular worry on your mind?
turns.patient_response:
Worried? Oh, heavens no. I don't really have anything to be anxious about these days. The house is paid for, the children are all settled... well, except for my grandson David, but he’s always been a bit of a rolling stone. He just moved to Seattle, actually. Or was it Portland? Somewhere out West where it rains all the time. I sent him a lovely yellow raincoat for his birthday, but I doubt he wears it. Young people today just don't seem to care about keeping dry, do they? They just walk right out in the drizzle in their sweatshirts. 

But no, it's not worry at all. It's just... well, it's just exactly like you said, a physical restlessness. Like when I'm at the senior center meetings, or trying to sit through the announcements at church. Pastor Miller is a dear, but his announcements can drag on for twenty minutes! I just get this terrible ants-in-my-chair feeling. I find myself shifting around, or I just have to stand up and go get a cup of coffee, or I start straightening the hymn books in the pew. The hymn books at our church are that lovely deep burgundy color, you know. They match the carpeting they put in back in 2012. I remember because the carpet layers made such a mess of the vestibule, we had to hold Sunday school in the basement for three weeks! But yes, I just have to move around to get through it. No worry, just... ants in my chair.

We put it in right after my husband got his promotion at the bank. He was so proud of that promotion. We celebrated by going to that nice Italian place downtown—Luigi's, I think it was called. He has such warm hands, which is a blessing. You know, usually doctors have freezing cold hands! I remember Dr. Gable, the doctor my family went to when I was a little girl in the thirties—his stethoscope was like a solid block of ice! We used to just dread going to see him in the wintertime. Winter seemed so much harsher back then, didn't it? We would get these enormous snowdrifts all the way up to the parlor windows. My older brother Thomas and I would build these massive snow forts out by the big oak tree. Thomas was always so terribly bossy about how the snow had to be packed down just perfectly or the walls would cave in. He ended up becoming an architect, so I suppose that makes sense! He actually helped design the public library over in Springfield. They have a lovely botanical garden in Springfield, right next to the library. The tulips in the spring are just breathtaking, they import the bulbs all the way from Holland. 

But... oh, I'm sorry, what was it you were asking? Right, the thyroid and the pills. No, nobody has ever told me my fidgeting is from a medical condition or my blood pressure pill or anything like that. I've just always been a person who needs to be up and doing!

I bought a box of the maple brown sugar ones when they were on sale at the Piggly Wiggly, but I ended up giving them to the food drive at church. Our church has a wonderful food pantry, you know. Mrs. Higgins runs it, and she is just a saint. She's been organizing it for at least fifteen years, ever since her husband passed away. He was a lovely man, played the organ on Sundays. He had the most magnificent booming voice when he sang the hymns. But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, yes, my blood pressure is just fine, and I feel perfectly normal with the pills.

The chalk dust used to get everywhere, all over my nice pleated skirts. My mother would be so annoyed when I came home covered in white dust. She used to scrub those skirts by hand in the sink with a bar of Fels-Naptha soap. You don't see Fels-Naptha much anymore, do you? It was the only thing that would get the grass stains out of my brother's trousers after he'd been playing baseball in the empty lot down the street. They paved over that lot years ago, put up a strip mall with a dry cleaner and a little bakery. The bakery has the most delightful lemon tarts... 

Oh, dear, I'm rambling again, aren't I? But no, to answer your question, I haven't been sick at all. No colds, no flu, nothing sudden like that. I've been perfectly healthy.
